Easy

1Easy

A consumer with u(x)=xu(x) = \sqrt{x}u(x)=x​ evaluates a lottery paying 144144144 with probability 1/21/21/2 and 363636 with probability 1/21/21/2.

Find the certainty equivalent and the risk premium.

c solves u(c)=U(L),premium=E[L]−cc \text{ solves } u(c) = U(L), \qquad \text{premium} = \mathbb{E}[L] - cc solves u(c)=U(L),premium=E[L]−c
  • Expected Utility
Show solution

  1. The expected value is E[L]=12⋅144+12⋅36=90\mathbb{E}[L] = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 144 + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 36 = 90E[L]=21​⋅144+21​⋅36=90. Expected utility is U(L)=12144+1236=12(12+6)=9U(L) = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{144} + \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{36} = \frac{1}{2}(12 + 6) = 9U(L)=21​144​+21​36​=21​(12+6)=9.

  2. The certainty equivalent solves c=9\sqrt{c} = 9c​=9, so c=81c = 81c=81. The risk premium is 90−81=990 - 81 = 990−81=9 — the consumer accepts a sure amount 9 below the expected value to shed the lottery.

2Medium

Show that in CRRA utility u(x)=x1−γ/(1−γ)u(x) = x^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)u(x)=x1−γ/(1−γ), the (normalized) utility converges to log utility as γ→1\gamma \to 1γ→1: lim⁡γ→1x1−γ−11−γ=ln⁡x\lim_{\gamma \to 1} \frac{x^{1-\gamma} - 1}{1-\gamma} = \ln xlimγ→1​1−γx1−γ−1​=lnx.

lim⁡γ→1x1−γ−11−γ=ln⁡x\lim_{\gamma \to 1} \frac{x^{1-\gamma} - 1}{1-\gamma} = \ln xγ→1lim​1−γx1−γ−1​=lnx
  • Measuring Risk Aversion
Show solution

  1. As γ→1\gamma \to 1γ→1, numerator and denominator both go to 000 — a 0/00/00/0 form. Apply l'Hôpital's rule in γ\gammaγ: the numerator's derivative is ddγ(x1−γ−1)=−x1−γln⁡x→−ln⁡x\frac{d}{d\gamma}(x^{1-\gamma} - 1) = -x^{1-\gamma}\ln x \to -\ln xdγd​(x1−γ−1)=−x1−γlnx→−lnx, the denominator's is −1-1−1.

  2. The limit is therefore (−ln⁡x)/(−1)=ln⁡x(-\ln x)/(-1) = \ln x(−lnx)/(−1)=lnx. For fixed γ\gammaγ, x1−γ/(1−γ)x^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)x1−γ/(1−γ) and (x1−γ−1)/(1−γ)(x^{1-\gamma}-1)/(1-\gamma)(x1−γ−1)/(1−γ) differ only by an affine transformation in xxx, hence represent the same preferences — which is why CRRA at γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1 is called log utility.

Differentiate expected utility with respect to β\betaβ to derive the first-order condition and solve for β∗(p)\beta^*(p)β∗(p).

Check the value at p=0.3p = 0.3p=0.3.

EU(β)=(1−π)W−pβ+πW−L+(1−p)βEU(\beta) = (1-\pi)\sqrt{W - p\beta} + \pi\sqrt{W - L + (1-p)\beta}EU(β)=(1−π)W−pβ​+πW−L+(1−p)β​

Show solution

  1. By the chain rule, d EUdβ=(1−π)−p2W1+π1−p2W2\frac{d\,EU}{d\beta} = (1-\pi)\frac{-p}{2\sqrt{W_1}} + \pi\frac{1-p}{2\sqrt{W_2}}dβdEU​=(1−π)2W1​​−p​+π2W2​​1−p​. Setting it to zero gives (1−π)pW1=π(1−p)W2\frac{(1-\pi)p}{\sqrt{W_1}} = \frac{\pi(1-p)}{\sqrt{W_2}}W1​​(1−π)p​=W2​​π(1−p)​ — marginal cost equals marginal benefit of the last dollar of coverage.

  2. Plugging in numbers: 0.7 p100−pβ=0.3 (1−p)40+(1−p)β\frac{0.7\,p}{\sqrt{100 - p\beta}} = \frac{0.3\,(1-p)}{\sqrt{40 + (1-p)\beta}}100−pβ​0.7p​=40+(1−p)β​0.3(1−p)​. Squaring both sides gives a quadratic in β\betaβ, but at p=0.3p = 0.3p=0.3 it collapses to 0.21W1=0.21W2\frac{0.21}{\sqrt{W_1}} = \frac{0.21}{\sqrt{W_2}}W1​​0.21​=W2​​0.21​, so W1=W2W_1 = W_2W1​=W2​ — i.e. 100−0.3β=40+0.7β100 - 0.3\beta = 40 + 0.7\beta100−0.3β=40+0.7β, giving β∗=60\beta^* = 60β∗=60.

    Full insurance is optimal at the fair premium.

Compute each certainty equivalent and risk premium, and explain via the Arrow-Pratt measure who is more risk averse.

c(γ)=[12⋅1501−γ+12⋅501−γ]11−γc(\gamma) = \left[\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 150^{1-\gamma} + \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 50^{1-\gamma}\right]^{\frac{1}{1-\gamma}}c(γ)=[21​⋅1501−γ+21​⋅501−γ]1−γ1​
rA(x)=γxr_A(x) = \frac{\gamma}{x}rA​(x)=xγ​
  • Expected Utility

Show solution

  1. With γA=0.5\gamma_A = 0.5γA​=0.5, cA=[12150+1250]2≈9.6592≈93.30c_A = \left[\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{150} + \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{50}\right]^2 \approx 9.659^2 \approx 93.30cA​=[21​150​+21​50​]2≈9.6592≈93.30. The risk premium is 100−93.30=6.70100 - 93.30 = 6.70100−93.30=6.70.

  2. With γB=2\gamma_B = 2γB​=2, 1−γ=−11-\gamma = -11−γ=−1, so cB=[12⋅150−1+12⋅50−1]−1=10.5/150+0.5/50=10.01333=75.0c_B = \left[\frac{1}{2} \cdot 150^{-1} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 50^{-1}\right]^{-1} = \frac{1}{0.5/150 + 0.5/50} = \frac{1}{0.01333} = 75.0cB​=[21​⋅150−1+21​⋅50−1]−1=0.5/150+0.5/501​=0.013331​=75.0. The risk premium 100−75=25.0100 - 75 = 25.0100−75=25.0 exceeds A's.

  3. The Arrow-Pratt measure is rA(x)=γ/xr_A(x) = \gamma/xrA​(x)=γ/x, so at x=100x = 100x=100, rAA=0.005r_A^A = 0.005rAA​=0.005 and rBA=0.02r_B^A = 0.02rBA​=0.02 — B is more risk averse at every wealth level, which shows up as a lower certainty equivalent and a larger risk premium. This matches the scene's observation that the CE drifts away from the expected value as γ\gammaγ rises.
